name: Dimensional Analysis
description: Using units to check if your physics equation is correct

content.overview: Here's a neat trick: you can catch a wrong equation just by looking at its units, before you even touch the numbers. That's dimensional analysis — a free error-detector hiding in plain sight. {{viz:diagram-01}}
content.explanation:
The core rule is simple: both sides of any physics equation have to end up with the same units. If they don't, you've got a problem. {{viz:diagram-02}}

**Quick check: does speed = distance ÷ time hold up?**

Left side: speed is in m/s
Right side: distance ÷ time = m ÷ s = m/s ✓

They match — so far so good.

**Now here's one that's broken:**

Say someone writes: distance = speed × speed

Left side: distance = meters (m)
Right side: speed × speed = (m/s) × (m/s) = m²/s²

m doesn't equal m²/s² — so this equation is flat-out wrong, no calculation needed to spot it. {{viz:anim-01}}

**How you actually use this:**

1. Write out the equation
2. Swap every variable for its units
3. Simplify the units like you'd simplify any fraction
4. See if both sides land on the same thing
5. If they don't — red flag, something's off

**Let's stress-test the famous one: does E = mc² check out?**

Left side: Energy is in joules, which is kg·m²/s²
Right side: m × c² = kg × (m/s)² = kg·m²/s²

They match! Dimensionally, this equation holds up. {{viz:chart-01}}

One caveat: matching units don't *prove* an equation is correct, but mismatched units definitely prove it's wrong. Think of dimensional analysis as your fast, free sanity check before you dive into the actual math.
keyPoints: Both sides of an equation need to land on the same units
Swap variables for their units and simplify like algebra
Units matching doesn't guarantee the equation is right, but mismatched units guarantee it's wrong
You can spot a broken equation before doing any real math
This is one of the fastest sanity checks in physics
Use it on every formula you're not 100% sure about
content.whyItMatters: Everyone messes up an equation now and then. Dimensional analysis is your 5-second gut check — 'wait, do these units even match?' — that saves you from confidently handing in a wrong answer.
